If you've ever wondered how bees sting, this is your lucky day.
Scientists use tiny images to find out the complex mechanism that makes the process work.
NPR's Yuki Noguchi has the details.
Scientists in Australia have been able to capture images of the inner workings of a
stinger, which is made up of a venom sac, a pumping chamber, and a pair of lancets that
help dig it deeper into the skin.
The key discovery is how the stinger operates, using a valve mechanism inside those lancets
to first inflate, then deflate in a pumping motion that also creates a kind of seal necessary
to deliver the venom, even if the stinger has detached from the bee.
Scientists say the research, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of
Sciences, might provide engineering inspiration for tiny pumps that could deliver medicines.
Yuki Noguchi, NPR News.
